answer:
URLSession is Apple's HTTP stack, and since Swift Concurrency arrived the everyday API is a pair of async methods that return `(Data, URLResponse)` and throw on failure.

- `data(from: url)` — a plain GET.
- `data(for: request)` — full control over method, headers and body.
- A session you configure yourself when you need timeouts, a cache policy, default headers or a delegate; `URLSession.shared` is fine for simple cases.

Two things the API deliberately does not do for you. A 404 or a 500 is a successful request, not a thrown error, so you have to cast the response to `HTTPURLResponse` and check `statusCode` yourself. And decoding is a separate step with `JSONDecoder`, which throws its own errors you should not merge with transport errors.

The old `dataTask(with:completionHandler:)` callbacks still exist and still work, but new code should not use them: they sit outside structured concurrency, so task cancellation never reaches them and every call site turns back into a completion-handler pyramid.

A reusable APIClient handles common concerns once: base URL, auth headers, retries, decoding, error mapping. Typical building blocks:

- **Endpoint type** — describes path, method, query, body. Often a protocol or struct.
- **Client** — takes Endpoint, executes URLRequest, decodes response.
- **Request modifiers** — interceptors (auth token, request id, log).
- **Error type** — typed `APIError` enum (network, decoding, status, server-message).

Keep the client untyped on body/response (Data) and let strongly-typed wrappers decode. Test by injecting a `protocol Networking` so you can swap a fake.

Cancellation and timeouts are separate mechanisms in Swift, and a solid client uses both: cancellation stops work you no longer want, timeouts stop work that is never coming back.

- **Task cancellation** — `task.cancel()` propagates into the underlying URLSessionTask; the async methods throw `CancellationError` or `URLError(.cancelled)` and the transfer stops. Structured children are cancelled with their parent, and `.task` on a SwiftUI view cancels when the view disappears.
- **Per-request timeout** — `URLRequest.timeoutInterval`, or on the session configuration `timeoutIntervalForRequest` (the gap allowed between bytes) and `timeoutIntervalForResource` (the ceiling for the whole transfer).
- **A manual deadline** — race the work against a sleeping task inside `withThrowingTaskGroup` when the API you are calling has no timeout of its own.

Two things that catch people out. Cancellation is cooperative, so a tight compute loop has to check `Task.isCancelled` itself. And a cancelled request is not a failure the user should see, which is why the catch block must separate `CancellationError` from real errors before showing an alert.

Debounce plus cancel-previous is the standard typeahead pattern: every keystroke cancels the in-flight task and starts a new one after a short sleep, so only the last query reaches the network.

One auth interceptor in the API client attaches the bearer token to every request and, on a 401, refreshes once and retries — no call site should ever know that tokens exist.

- Store the access and refresh tokens in the Keychain, never in UserDefaults.
- The refresh call itself must bypass the interceptor, or a failing refresh will 401 and trigger another refresh forever.
- **Refresh must be concurrency-safe**: five requests failing at once should share one refresh, not fire five. An `actor` holding the in-flight refresh `Task` is the idiomatic Swift answer, and it is usually the point of the question.
- Retry exactly once. If the refresh itself fails, clear the Keychain and route to login.
- Do not blindly replay non-idempotent requests — a POST that already reached the server should not be sent twice.

URLSession's authentication challenge delegate covers HTTP Basic and Digest, but for bearer-token APIs an interceptor in your own client is simpler, easier to test, and the only place that can coordinate a shared refresh.

URLSession has no multipart builder, so you assemble the body yourself: a unique boundary string, one part per field carrying its own Content-Disposition header, and a closing boundary that ends in two extra dashes.

- `upload(for:from:)` — the async method for a body you already hold in memory; it returns `(Data, URLResponse)` just like `data(for:)`.
- `upload(for:fromFile:)` — streams from disk instead of loading the file into memory, which is what you want for anything camera-sized.
- Set the request's Content-Type to `multipart/form-data; boundary=<your boundary>`, and use CRLF line endings inside the body — a bare newline is rejected by many servers.
- For progress, pass a `URLSessionTaskDelegate` to the async upload call and implement `didSendBodyData`.
- For an upload that must survive the app being suspended, build the session from `URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier:)`. Background sessions accept file-based uploads only, never in-memory Data, and completion arrives through the delegate after relaunch.

Hand-built bodies fail in exactly two places: a missing CRLF before the closing boundary, and holding a large file in Data on a memory-tight device.

Certificate pinning hardens TLS by trusting only specific server certificates / public keys, defending against MITM with rogue CAs.

- Pin the leaf or intermediate certificate (rotate when server rotates).
- Pin the public key (rotation-friendly — only when the team rotates the keypair).
- App Transport Security (ATS) provides pinning via `NSPinnedDomains` plist (iOS 14+).
- **Manual**: implement `urlSession(_:didReceive:completionHandler:)` and validate the server trust against a bundled certificate hash.
- **Always plan for rotation** — bundle multiple pins, ship a kill-switch, keep an out-of-band update path.

URLSession already ships an HTTP cache, and most apps get nothing from it because the server sends no validators and the client never asks for one.

- `URLCache` is active on a default session: a response carrying `Cache-Control` or `Expires` is replayed from memory or disk with no round trip at all. Size it yourself with `URLCache(memoryCapacity:diskCapacity:directory:)` on the configuration, because the default disk budget is small.
- Validation is the other half. Keep the `ETag` (or `Last-Modified`) from the last response and send it back as `If-None-Match` (or `If-Modified-Since`); the server answers 304 with no body, so you pay one small round trip instead of the payload.
- `URLRequest.cachePolicy` picks behaviour per request: the default honours the headers, `.reloadIgnoringLocalCacheData` is right for pull-to-refresh and for a request where you are doing the validation yourself, `.returnCacheDataElseLoad` gives an instant first paint.
- **Know the exclusions**: ephemeral sessions keep nothing, background sessions do not use it the same way, POST responses are not cached, and the cache is cleared whenever the app is deleted.
- The HTTP cache is a bandwidth optimisation, not offline support. Content the user must still see tomorrow belongs in your own store.

The follow-up an interviewer usually asks is the difference between freshness and validation: `max-age` skips the request entirely, an ETag still costs a request but saves the body.

Retry only failures a later attempt could plausibly fix, and space attempts with exponential backoff plus random jitter so a recovering server is not hit by every device at the same instant.

- **Retryable** — transport failures such as timeouts and a dropped connection, plus 5xx and 429 from the server. When the response carries `Retry-After`, honour it instead of your own schedule.
- **Not retryable** — the 4xx family that describes your request: 400, 403, 404, 422. A 401 is not a retry either, it is a token refresh followed by one replay.
- **Backoff** — wait base times two to the power of the attempt, capped at a few seconds, then add random jitter. Without jitter every client that failed together retries together and the outage repeats.
- **Idempotency** — GET, PUT and DELETE are safe to repeat, POST is not. For payments or order creation send an idempotency key the server can de-duplicate on, then retrying is safe.
- **Bound it** — two or three attempts, one overall deadline, and no further attempt once the task is cancelled. Check cancellation across the sleep so a dismissed screen stops retrying.
- Do not stack retries in layers: three in the client times three in the repository times three in the UI is twenty-seven requests for one tap.

Let the request wait instead of pre-checking the network: with `waitsForConnectivity` set on the configuration, URLSession holds the task until a usable path appears rather than failing immediately.

- Pair it with `timeoutIntervalForResource` as the ceiling for the whole transfer, and implement `urlSession(_:taskIsWaitingForConnectivity:)` as the cue to show an offline banner instead of an error alert.
- Never gate a call behind a reachability check. Reachability describes the past, not whether this request will succeed, and a captive portal reports a perfectly good path.
- `NWPathMonitor` from the Network framework is the current API for observing connectivity, and it is for UI decisions — an offline banner, a disabled Send button, resuming a queue — not for guarding every request.
- Separate the errors that mean try later, `notConnectedToInternet` and `networkConnectionLost`, from real failures; only the first group belongs in a retry queue.
- Queue the user's writes locally and replay them when the path returns, showing a pending state rather than throwing the work away.
- `allowsExpensiveNetworkAccess` and `allowsConstrainedNetworkAccess` keep big transfers off cellular and off Low Data Mode.

A background session hands the transfer to a system daemon that keeps working while your app is suspended or terminated, and reports back by relaunching the app.

- Build it from `URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier:)`, one identifier per session, and keep a single instance for that identifier — creating a second one with the same id traps.
- Background sessions are delegate-only. There is no async `data(for:)` and no completion handler, so you implement `URLSessionDownloadDelegate` and move the file out of the temporary URL inside `didFinishDownloadingTo` synchronously, because the system deletes it as soon as that method returns.
- Uploads must come from a file, never from in-memory `Data`.
- Relaunch handling is the part people forget: the system calls `application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:)`, you store that handler, recreate the session with the same identifier, and call the handler on the main queue from `urlSessionDidFinishEvents`.
- The system decides when the transfer actually runs, guided by power and network conditions; `isDiscretionary` and `earliestBeginDate` express preferences, so never promise the user a completion time.
- Progress arrives through `didWriteData`, and a cancelled download can resume later through `cancel(byProducingResumeData:)` and `downloadTask(withResumeData:)`.

Two traps worth naming: `URLSession.shared` cannot do any of this, and after a relaunch there is no view controller waiting, so all the state the delegate needs must already be on disk.

`URLSessionWebSocketTask` gives you a connection with send and receive, and nothing else — the read loop, the keepalive and the reconnect logic are all yours to write.

- `webSocketTask(with:)` then `resume()` opens the socket, `send(.string)` or `send(.data)` writes, and `receive()` delivers exactly one message, so you must call it again for the next one.
- Wrap that loop in an `AsyncThrowingStream` so the screen can `for await` the messages and so cancelling the consuming task tears the socket down with it.
- Keep it alive with `sendPing(pongReceiveHandler:)` on a timer; intermediaries routinely drop a socket that has been idle for under a minute.
- Reconnect with backoff and jitter, and resubscribe after every reconnect. A client that silently reconnects but never re-sends its subscriptions is the classic production bug, so also request whatever was missed by sequence number.
- **Handle backgrounding**: iOS suspends the socket, so reconnect when the app returns to the foreground instead of assuming it survived. Close politely with `cancel(with: .goingAway, reason: nil)`.
- Pick the transport deliberately. For one-way updates server-sent events or polling are cheaper to run, and only a push notification reaches a user whose app is not running.

Two techniques cover it: inject a protocol you can fake when you are testing your own client, and register a `URLProtocol` subclass when the real URL loading path is what you need to exercise.

- **Protocol injection** — declare a tiny `HTTPClient` protocol with the one method you use, conform `URLSession` to it in production and pass a stub in tests. Fast, synchronous to set up, and the default choice for testing your repository or view model.
- `URLProtocol` stub — subclass it, return canned `Data` and an `HTTPURLResponse` from `startLoading()`, and install it through `configuration.protocolClasses`. This is the only way to test the code that actually builds requests, so headers, cache policy and status-code mapping are covered.
- Build the session from a fresh `URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral` in each test rather than registering the stub globally, otherwise stubs leak between tests and failures become order-dependent.
- Test the paths that really break: a 500, a 204 with an empty body, malformed JSON, a `URLError(.timedOut)`, and cancellation midway.
- Keep decoding contract tests over recorded fixtures so a server-side rename fails the suite, and keep live-network tests out of the unit suite entirely.

The query was pasted into a string, so `URL(string:)` either returned nil or handed the server a value it read as extra parameters — queries are built from `URLComponents` and `URLQueryItem`, never by interpolation.

- `URL(string:)` is a parser, not an encoder. `#` starts the fragment, so `q=C#` sends `C`; `&` starts the next parameter; a raw space makes the initialiser return nil, and the `!` after it is the crash in your logs.
- `URLComponents.queryItems` percent-encodes every name and value for you and assembles them in order, so `C++ & Swift` arrives as one value.
- **The one gap is `+`**: it is a legal character inside a query, so `URLComponents` leaves it alone, and a server decoding the query as form data reads it back as a space. Patch `percentEncodedQuery` after setting `queryItems`.
- `addingPercentEncoding(withAllowedCharacters: .urlQueryAllowed)` is not the fix — that character set allows `&`, `=` and `+`, exactly the characters that break a value.
- Path segments need encoding too: `appending(path:)` escapes what you hand it, interpolation into the path string does not.
- Read the request back with `request.url?.absoluteString` when you are unsure; what the server sees is that string, not the array you built.

Rule of thumb: the only piece of a URL you are allowed to concatenate is your own path template. Anything a user typed goes through `URLQueryItem`.

`.iso8601` is `ISO8601DateFormatter` with its default options, and those do not include fractional seconds, so `2026-03-01T12:00:00.123Z` throws while `2026-03-01T12:00:00Z` decodes.

- The fix is a `.custom` strategy backed by an `ISO8601DateFormatter` whose `formatOptions` are `[.withInternetDateTime, .withFractionalSeconds]`, or `Date.ISO8601FormatStyle(includingFractionalSeconds: true)`.
- Accept both shapes. Many backends drop a `.000`, so a strategy that only understands fractional seconds fails on exactly the rows that land on a whole second — try the fractional formatter first, then the plain one.
- For a format that is not ISO at all, `DateFormatter` needs `locale = Locale(identifier: "en_US_POSIX")` and an explicit `timeZone`. Without the POSIX locale, a device on a 12-hour clock or a non-Gregorian calendar parses `HH:mm:ss` differently and every date fails — for that user only, which is why it survives review.
- Formatters and decoders are expensive to build. Create one configured `JSONDecoder` per client and share it; building one per response is a routine profiling finding on list screens.
- The neighbouring trap: with `keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase` the key is already `createdAt` by the time your `CodingKeys` are matched, so writing `case createdAt = "created_at"` matches nothing and throws `keyNotFound`.
- Encode with the mirror strategy, or a round trip through your own disk cache quietly rewrites the timestamps.

Mental model: `Codable` gives you the plumbing, the strategies are the contract with that specific server — pin them once, next to the client.

It is creating a `URLSession` per request: each session brings its own connection pool, cache and cookie storage, so nothing is ever reused, and a session created with a delegate holds that delegate strongly until you invalidate it.

- `URLSession` is designed to be long-lived — one per configuration, held for the lifetime of the app or the feature. Requests are cheap; sessions are not.
- The connection pool belongs to the session. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TLS connection, and reuse is what removes the handshake round trips you are watching in the trace. A per-request session throws that away every time.
- **The leak**: `URLSession(configuration:delegate:delegateQueue:)` retains the delegate, and the delegate usually retains the session back through a `lazy var`. Neither is freed until `finishTasksAndInvalidate()` (let running tasks finish) or `invalidateAndCancel()` (kill them now).
- The `URLCache`, `HTTPCookieStorage` and credential storage also hang off the session, so a per-request session cannot benefit from 304s or keep a login cookie either.
- `URLSession.shared` is fine for a plain GET but takes no delegate and no configuration — the moment you need timeouts, pinning or background transfers you own a configured session.
- Since iOS 15 you rarely need a session delegate at all: `session.data(for:delegate:)` attaches a per-task delegate, retained only until that task finishes.

Mental model: sessions are connection pools, not requests. Build them where you build your API client, and invalidate at an explicit teardown point.

Decoding an array is all-or-nothing: `JSONDecoder` throws on the first element it cannot build and you lose the other forty-nine, so make unknown values decodable and isolate the failure to a single element.

- A `String`-backed enum gets a synthesised `init(from:)` that throws `dataCorrupted` for any raw value it does not know. Write the initialiser yourself and fall back to an `unknown` case; that alone fixes most "server shipped a new type" outages.
- For everything else, decode the array through a wrapper that catches per element and keeps the rest. **The trap inside that wrapper**: a failed `decode` does not advance `currentIndex` in an `UnkeyedDecodingContainer`, so you must consume the bad element with a throwaway `Decodable` or the loop spins forever.
- Optional plus a default beats a non-optional field for anything the server might stop sending; `decodeIfPresent` and a `??` are cheaper than an outage.
- Log what you dropped. `DecodingError`'s `codingPath` names the index and the key — "the data couldn't be read" without it is unactionable, and the count of dropped rows is the metric that tells you the contract broke.
- Be liberal only where being liberal is safe. Skipping a feed card is fine; silently skipping a transaction or a permission flag is worse than a visible error, so keep those fields required and let the request fail loudly.

Rule of thumb: tolerate unknown values, never tolerate unknown meaning.

`data(for:)` buffers the whole body in memory before it returns, while `bytes(for:)` hands you the response as an `AsyncSequence` you consume as it arrives, so peak memory is one record instead of the entire payload.

- `let (bytes, response) = try await session.bytes(for: request)` gives a `URLSession.AsyncBytes`. Check the `HTTPURLResponse` status before you start consuming: an error body is not what your row decoder expects.
- `bytes.lines` is an `AsyncSequence` of `String`, which is exactly the shape of NDJSON and of server-sent events, where each event is a run of `data:` lines ended by a blank line.
- Backpressure is real. The sequence only reads ahead a little, so a slow consumer slows the transfer instead of inflating memory — and breaking out of the `for try await` loop, or cancelling the task, cancels the underlying `URLSessionTask`.
- **The trap is what you do inside the loop**: appending every decoded row to one array is `data(for:)` with extra steps, and writing each row to the store on the main actor turns a memory problem into a frozen UI. Batch a few hundred rows and write them off the main actor.
- If the payload is a file rather than records, do not stream it by hand: `download(for:)` writes straight to disk and gives you a URL, and it is the only shape that works in a background session.

Rule of thumb: memory should scale with one record, never with the response.

Everything the session owns outlives your token wipe: `URLCache` still holds the response bodies on disk, `HTTPCookieStorage` still holds the session cookie, and in-flight tasks started by the previous user are still running — clearing the Keychain touches none of it.

- Cached bodies come back first. A response with `Cache-Control: max-age` is replayed from `URLCache` with no round trip at all, so the new user sees the old feed. Call `removeAllCachedResponses()` on the session's cache, not just on `URLCache.shared`.
- Cookies are per configuration and persist across launches on a `.default` session, so a server that authenticates by cookie keeps authenticating the old identity. Delete them, and clear `URLCredentialStorage` for Basic or client-certificate auth.
- **Cancel before you clear.** A request that was already in flight will finish and write the previous user's data into the new user's store — `invalidateAndCancel()` kills the tasks and the pooled connections, and you then build a fresh session.
- `session.reset { }` does cookies, cache and credentials in one call when you want to keep the session object.
- Prevention beats cleanup: mark per-user responses `no-store` on the server, or run the authenticated session on `URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral` so nothing reaches disk in the first place.
- Your own layers count too — image caches, decoded model caches, the local database, and any `Task` a screen left running.

Mental model: logging out is a teardown of the whole networking stack, not the deletion of a token.

Model each concern as a middleware that receives the request plus a `next` closure it must call, then fold the array into one send function — the position in the array is the nesting order, and the nesting order is the behaviour.

- The shape is one method: `intercept(_ request: URLRequest, next: Send) async throws -> (Data, HTTPURLResponse)`, where `Send` is the same signature. A middleware may modify the request, call `next` zero, one or many times, and modify or replace what comes back.
- Compose by folding the array from the back over the transport closure, so element zero ends up outermost. That single `reduce` replaces the chain of wrapper classes people usually write.
- **Order is the design.** Retry outside auth replays with the stale token that caused the 401; auth outside retry refreshes once and every attempt carries a fresh header. Logging outermost sees one line per call, innermost sees one per attempt, and metrics have to sit against the transport to time the real transfer.
- A middleware that starts a *different* request — refreshing a token, fetching a config — must call the transport directly, never `next`, or it re-enters the whole chain and can loop forever.
- Middlewares are shared across concurrent tasks, so they are `Sendable` values; anything mutable (the token, a retry budget) lives in an actor behind them.
- `URLProtocol` is the wrong tool for this in production: it sits below the session, is registered globally, and cannot cleanly await your actors. Keep it for tests.

Rule of thumb: one array declares the whole request pipeline, and reading it top to bottom tells you what happens to a request.

URLSession follows redirects automatically, and for a 301, 302 or 303 the follow-up request is rewritten as a GET with the body dropped — curl never followed the redirect at all unless you passed `-L`.

- The mechanism: the system builds the new request itself, follows a bounded number of hops and then fails with `URLError.httpTooManyRedirects`. Everything after the first hop happens without your code being consulted, which is why the symptom is invisible in your own logging.
- 307 and 308 preserve the method and the body. If an API endpoint genuinely moved, that is the status to ask the backend for — or better, stop redirecting writes at all.
- The single hook is the task delegate `urlSession(_:task:willPerformHTTPRedirection:newRequest:)`. Return `newRequest` to follow it, a modified request to adjust it, or `nil` to stop, in which case the 3xx arrives as your response and you can fail loudly instead of silently doing nothing.
- Since iOS 15 an async call still gets that hook: pass a per-task delegate to `session.data(for:delegate:)`.
- **The security half**: the system-built request carries your headers, `Authorization` included, to the redirect target — which may be a different host. Strip credentials in the delegate whenever the host changes.
- If you rebuild the request yourself, remember the body is gone: setting `httpMethod` back to POST without re-attaching `httpBody` sends an empty POST, which is a subtler version of the same bug.

Rule of thumb: a non-idempotent request should never be redirected silently. Decide in the delegate, or make the server stop.
